title: Shadow Tracker
intro: Move the Sun across the sky and record the stick's shadow, place the constellations in their seasons, and pick which way down points on a globe. Then read the patterns you just built.
note: This is a model that uses the lesson's backup data (the 10 cm stick shadow table and the monthly constellation chart). The real shadow clock from the lesson still counts. The pictures are simple sketches.
summary: Shadows are long in the morning and evening, shortest near noon, and always point away from the Sun: west in the morning, north at noon, east in the afternoon, because Earth rotates. Earth orbits the Sun, so different constellations appear in different seasons. Gravity pulls every object down, toward the center of Earth, wherever you stand.

rounds.question: A 10 cm stick stands on flat ground in Michigan on a sunny spring or fall day. What happens to its shadow?
rounds.logTitle: Shadow table (10 cm stick, a sunny spring or fall day in Michigan)

reads.q: Look at the table. When is the shadow shortest?

choices.label: Near noon, when the Sun is highest
choices.why: Yes. 12:00 pm is 9 cm, the shortest of the day.

choices.label: In the morning
choices.why: At 8:30 am the shadow is 34 cm, the longest. Look for the smallest number.

choices.label: The shadow stays the same length all day
choices.why: The lengths run 34, 20, 9, 18, 30 cm. They change in a pattern.

reads.q: Which way does the shadow point?

choices.label: Away from the Sun: west in the morning, north at noon, east in the afternoon
choices.why: Yes. Look at the shadow map: the shadow is always opposite the Sun.

choices.label: Toward the Sun
choices.why: Look at the map: the shadow is on the opposite side of the stick from the Sun.

choices.label: Always north
choices.why: Only the noon shadow points north. Morning points west and afternoon points east.

reads.q: Why does the shadow pattern repeat every day?

choices.label: Earth rotates once each day
choices.why: Yes. Earth's spin makes the Sun appear to cross the sky, so shadows swing and shrink and grow the same way each day.

choices.label: The Sun travels around Earth each day
choices.why: It is Earth's rotation. The Sun only appears to move across the sky.

choices.label: Clouds push the shadow around
choices.why: This is a sunny-day table with no clouds, and the pattern is the same every sunny day.

choices.label: a stick's shadow at five times of day
choices.why: Right. 8:30 am, 10:00 am, 12:00 pm, 2:00 pm and 3:30 pm.

choices.label: the shadow only at noon
choices.why: The table has five times, not one. One measurement would not show a pattern.

choices.label: the shadow was longest morning and evening, shortest at noon, always pointing away from the Sun
choices.why: Yes. 34, 20, 9, 18, 30 cm: west, northwest, north, northeast, east.

choices.label: the shadow stayed one length and one direction
choices.why: The lengths and directions in the table all change, in a pattern.

choices.label: Earth's rotation makes a daily shadow pattern we can predict
choices.why: Yes. The same pattern repeats every sunny day, which is how a shadow clock works.

choices.label: shadows change at random
choices.why: The table is a pattern, not random: long, shorter, shortest, longer, long.

rounds.question: Why do different constellations appear in different seasons?

cards.name: Orion
cards.hint: this one is often easy to find on a clear Michigan winter night.
cards.why: Orion is often seen on winter nights, Dec-Feb.

cards.name: Leo
cards.hint: this one belongs to the months right after winter ends.
cards.why: Leo is often seen on spring nights, Mar-May.

cards.name: Scorpius
cards.hint: this one belongs to the months with the shortest nights of the year.
cards.why: Scorpius is often seen on summer nights, Jun-Aug.

cards.name: Cygnus
cards.hint: this one belongs to the months when school starts again.
cards.why: Cygnus is often seen on fall nights, Sep-Nov.

reads.q: Why do we see Orion in winter and Scorpius in summer?

choices.label: Earth orbits the Sun, so our night side faces different star groups
choices.why: Yes. As Earth moves around the Sun, the night side of Earth points toward different stars.

choices.label: Some stars turn off in summer
choices.why: Stars do not turn off. Our night side faces a different direction in each season.

choices.label: Earth is closer to Orion in winter
choices.why: Stars are very far away. Our night side faces a different star group as Earth orbits the Sun.

reads.q: The Sun looks much brighter than Orion's stars. Why?

choices.label: The Sun is much closer to us than any other star
choices.why: Yes. The Sun is not the biggest star; it looks brightest because it is the closest.

choices.label: The Sun is the biggest star
choices.why: Some far stars give off more light than the Sun, but they are too far away to look bright.

choices.label: The Sun is the only star that makes light
choices.why: Every star makes light. The Sun just looks brighter because it is so close.

choices.label: Orion, Leo, Scorpius and Cygnus in their seasons
choices.why: Right. Winter, spring, summer and fall each have their own constellation.

choices.label: every constellation in every season
choices.why: Each card belongs to one season. The night sky changes through the year.

choices.label: the night sky changes as Earth orbits the Sun
choices.why: Yes. Different seasons, different constellations.

choices.label: the same stars all year
choices.why: The chart shows different constellations for different months.

choices.label: Earth's orbit makes a seasonal star pattern we can predict
choices.why: Yes. The pattern repeats every year, so we know when to look for Orion.

choices.label: stars appear in seasons by luck
choices.why: The chart is a repeating pattern, not luck.

rounds.question: Which way is down, wherever you stand on Earth?

spots.label: standing at the top of the globe

choices.label: Toward the center of Earth
choices.why: Yes. Down means toward Earth's center, wherever you stand.

choices.label: Up into the sky
choices.why: That way things would fall into the sky. Dropped things fall toward the ground under your feet, which is toward Earth's center.

choices.label: Sideways
choices.why: A dropped ball falls straight down, toward the ground under your feet, not sideways.

spots.label: standing at the bottom of the globe

choices.label: Toward the center of Earth
choices.why: Yes. At the bottom of the globe, down still means toward Earth's center. People there do not fall off.

choices.label: Away from the center, off the bottom
choices.why: Then everything there would fall off Earth. It does not; their down points toward the center, just like yours.

choices.label: Gravity needs air, so there is no down there
choices.why: Gravity works even without air. It pulls everywhere on Earth.

spots.label: standing on the side of the globe

choices.label: Toward the center of Earth
choices.why: Yes. Every arrow points to the center. That is what down means.

choices.label: Toward the bottom of the picture
choices.why: Down is not about the picture. It is toward Earth's center, wherever you stand.

choices.label: Out into space
choices.why: Things fall to the ground, not into space. Their down points at the center.

reads.q: What do all three arrows have in common?

choices.label: Every arrow points toward the center of Earth
choices.why: Yes. Down means toward Earth's center, wherever you stand.

choices.label: Every arrow points the same way on the picture
choices.why: The arrows point different ways on the picture, but the same way on the globe: to the center.

choices.label: Gravity only works at the top of the globe
choices.why: Gravity pulls everywhere. That is why all three spots have a down.

reads.q: You drop a ball, toss it up, and toss it sideways. What happens each time?

choices.label: It comes back down every time
choices.why: Yes. That matches the lesson's toss table: no matter how you toss it, it comes back down.

choices.label: The sideways toss keeps going forever
choices.why: Gravity keeps pulling it toward Earth's center, so it comes down too.

choices.label: The tossed-up ball stays up
choices.why: It slows, stops and comes back down. Gravity never stops pulling.

choices.label: down arrows at three spots on a globe
choices.why: Right. Top, bottom and side.

choices.label: arrows only where we live
choices.why: We placed arrows all around the globe, not just in one place.

choices.label: every arrow pointed toward the center of Earth
choices.why: Yes. Look at the globe: all three arrows aim at the middle.

choices.label: the arrows pointed every which way
choices.why: They look different on the page, but each one points to the center.

choices.label: Earth's gravity pulls objects down, toward Earth's center, wherever you stand
choices.why: Yes. That is the argument the toss table supports too: no matter how you toss it, it comes back down.

choices.label: gravity pulls toward the nearest picture edge
choices.why: Down is toward Earth's center, not the bottom of a drawing.
